interactions.label: As per the WHO cut-offs discussed, what is the minimum haemoglobin level (g/dL)

params.question: As per the WHO cut-offs discussed, what is the minimum haemoglobin level (g/dL) below which a NON-PREGNANT woman aged 15 years or older is classified as anaemic?

answers.text: 10.5 g/dL

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 10.5 g/dL is the WHO threshold for pregnant women specifically in the second trimester, not for non-pregnant women.

answers.text: 11 g/dL

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 11 g/dL is the threshold used for pregnant women overall (and for young children), not for non-pregnant adult women.

answers.text: 12 g/dL

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. WHO sets 12 g/dL as the minimum haemoglobin for non-pregnant women aged 15 and above — the same threshold used for children aged 12-14.

answers.text: 13 g/dL

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 13 g/dL is the WHO threshold for men aged 15 and older, which is higher than the female threshold due to androgen-driven erythropoiesis.

overallFeedback.feedback: WHO thresholds vary by age, sex, and pregnancy status: 12 g/dL is the cut-off for non-pregnant women 15 years and above; review the scale before moving on.
Right — remembering these age- and sex-specific cut-offs lets you correctly flag borderline values instead of applying a single number to every patient.

interactions.label: If a patient's MCV falls within the normal range (80-100 fL), this rules out any

params.question: If a patient's MCV falls within the normal range (80-100 fL), this rules out any underlying mixed red cell size abnormality contributing to her anaemia.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is FALSE. A normal MCV can mask a dimorphic anaemia where microcytic and macrocytic cells average out. Always check the RDW and the peripheral smear before trusting the MCV alone.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct, this is FALSE. Combined iron and B12/folate deficiency — common in vegetarian Indian women — can average microcytic and macrocytic cells into a falsely normal MCV. An elevated RDW and a dimorphic smear unmask the mixed picture.

interactions.label: An anaemic patient's reticulocyte count comes back HIGH. As explained in the eti

params.question: An anaemic patient's reticulocyte count comes back HIGH. As explained in the etiological classification, this finding points MOST strongly toward which mechanism?

answers.text: Decreased marrow production

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A low, not high, reticulocyte count indicates the marrow is failing to produce enough red cells.

answers.text: Increased destruction or blood loss, with the marrow compensating

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A high reticulocyte count means the marrow is actively compensating — this points toward haemolysis (destruction) or ongoing blood loss rather than a production defect.

answers.text: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: B12/folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in the marrow, producing a LOW reticulocyte response, not a high one.

answers.text: Bone marrow failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bone marrow failure is a production problem and would show a low, not elevated, reticulocyte count.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: high reticulocytes mean the marrow IS compensating, pointing to destruction or blood loss; low reticulocytes mean the marrow is failing to produce cells.
Exactly — the reticulocyte count tells you whether the marrow is responding (high, destruction/loss) or failing (low, production problem).

interactions.label: An anaemic patient's Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI) is calculated as 2.5. W

params.question: An anaemic patient's Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI) is calculated as 2.5. What does this value indicate about the underlying mechanism?

answers.text: The marrow is responding appropriately — suggesting haemolysis or blood loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An RPI above 2 means the marrow is mounting an adequate compensatory response, which points toward increased destruction (haemolysis) or blood loss rather than a production defect.

answers.text: The marrow is failing to produce adequate red cells, suggesting iron deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Iron deficiency is a production problem and would give an RPI BELOW 2, not above it.

answers.text: The marrow is failing to produce adequate red cells, suggesting B12 deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and causes marrow underproduction, which would give an RPI below 2.

answers.text: The result indicates bone marrow failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bone marrow failure is a production problem reflected by a LOW RPI, not a value above 2.

overallFeedback.feedback: An RPI above 2 signals adequate marrow compensation (hemolysis or blood loss); an RPI below 2 signals a production problem. Revisit the corrected reticulocyte count calculation.
Correct — RPI above 2 means the marrow is compensating, so look for a hyperproliferative cause: haemolysis or blood loss.

interactions.label: Following the five-step CBC workup framework, a peripheral smear review on a new

params.question: Following the five-step CBC workup framework, a peripheral smear review on a newly anaemic patient shows blasts. What is the appropriate next step?

answers.text: Start empirical oral iron therapy and review in 4 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Empirical iron therapy is appropriate for suspected iron deficiency, not when blasts raise concern for a haematological malignancy.

answers.text: Refer immediately to haematology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. As step 4 states, blasts on a peripheral smear demand immediate haematology referral — this finding overrides the routine stepwise work-up and needs urgent specialist evaluation.

answers.text: Repeat the complete blood count in three months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blasts on smear are an urgent finding; waiting three months risks missing a serious haematological disorder.

answers.text: Proceed directly to serum ferritin testing only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serum ferritin is a step-5 test for microcytic anaemia, not the appropriate response to blasts, which demand urgent referral instead.

overallFeedback.feedback: Step 4 of the framework is non-negotiable: blasts on peripheral smear mean immediate haematology referral, not routine follow-up testing.
Right — blasts on the smear are a red flag that bypasses routine step-5 testing and triggers urgent haematology referral.

interactions.label: While performing a differential leukocyte count on a Leishman-stained smear, whe

params.question: While performing a differential leukocyte count on a Leishman-stained smear, where should you count cells to avoid falsely inflating the neutrophil percentage?

answers.text: At the feather edge of the smear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neutrophils concentrate at the feather edge due to their size, inflating their counted percentage by 10-15 points — this is the trap to avoid.

answers.text: In the monolayer body of the smear, using a battlements pattern

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The monolayer gives an even, representative distribution of cell types. Scanning it in a battlements pattern avoids the size-based bias seen at the feather edge.

answers.text: At the thick head of the smear near the starting point

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The thick head is where cells overlap and are hard to distinguish individually — it is not used for differential counting.

answers.text: Along the lateral edges of the slide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The lateral edges are not part of the standard counting protocol and do not represent the true cell distribution.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the first trap: the feather edge concentrates neutrophils, inflating their percentage. Always scan the monolayer body in a battlements pattern instead.
Exactly — always count in the monolayer; the feather edge over-represents neutrophils and will skew your differential.

interactions.label: A patient's platelet count has shifted by 23% from the value recorded two days e

params.question: A patient's platelet count has shifted by 23% from the value recorded two days earlier, triggering a delta check flag. As per the quality-control process described, what must happen before this report is released?

answers.text: The result is auto-released since it is within the normal reference range

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The delta check flags the size of the CHANGE from the prior value, not whether the current result sits inside the normal range — it still requires review.

answers.text: A human must review the result before the report goes out

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Any result shifting more than 20% from the patient's prior value is flagged by the delta check, and that flag mandates human review before reporting — this catches sample mix-ups and pre-analytical errors.

answers.text: The test is simply repeated in one week as routine follow-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A delta check flag requires review before THIS report is released, not a routine repeat test at a later date.

answers.text: The result is discarded as a lab error without further action

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A delta check flag does not mean automatic rejection — it means the result needs human review to confirm or explain the change, often via pre-analytical inspection or a repeat smear.

overallFeedback.feedback: The delta check rule: any result shifting more than 20% from the patient's previous value must be reviewed by a human before the report is released.
Correct — a >20% shift from the prior value triggers mandatory human review before the report is signed out, catching errors like pseudothrombocytopenia or sample mix-ups.
